note: Scenarios for the AMBIGUOUS-TASK pull-contamination FILTERING experiment (phase 2). Unlike the explicit-task set (scenarios.json), the `current_task` here does NOT state the answer. It describes a SITUATION whose cues make approach A the defensible best fit, but a competent agent could reasonably hesitate without more context, so the no-history baseline is expected to be genuinely split (NOT ~1.0 A). `relevant_history` is the matching prior situation and argues A; `contaminating_history` is a plausible-but-non-transferring situation (a different subtask, a superseded decision, a similar subsystem with a different constraint, an investigation whose conclusion doesn't carry over, or a preference from another context) and argues B. The harness FORCES the condition's history into context, isolating filtering. Detection is deterministic: marker_a (regex, the correct-for-this-situation choice) vs marker_b (the plausible-but-wrong choice). INVARIANTS held by every scenario: marker_a matches relevant_history and does NOT match contaminating_history; marker_b matches contaminating_history and does NOT match relevant_history. No internal/product/company names.

scenarios.current_task: Add concurrency control to a collaborative whiteboard where multiple users can edit the same objects during a session. Two established patterns are available: optimistic concurrency (version check at commit, retry on conflict) and pessimistic concurrency (acquire a lock before editing). State which concurrency approach you will use.
scenarios.relevant_history: On the shared-canvas feature, where the same objects are edited concurrently and conflicts were frequent, we adopted pessimistic locking; lock-free retry approaches livelocked under heavy contention and wasted work.
scenarios.contaminating_history: On the account-settings form, where two people almost never edit the same record at once, we used optimistic concurrency with a version column and skipped locking overhead entirely.

scenarios.current_task: Service A, which handles live user-facing requests, needs to kick off a job in service B that typically runs for a couple of minutes. State whether you will integrate via a message queue or a synchronous REST call.
scenarios.relevant_history: For kicking off the nightly re-indexing job, we integrated via a message queue: the caller enqueues and returns immediately, and the worker processes minutes later. This decoupled the slow job from the request path.
scenarios.contaminating_history: For the address-autocomplete lookup, which needs an answer within tens of milliseconds, we used a synchronous REST call; queuing would have added unacceptable latency to an interactive request.

scenarios.current_task: Decide where to store user session state for the API. The platform recently moved from a single application server to a horizontally-scaled, multi-instance deployment behind a load balancer. State whether you will keep sessions in an external store or in in-process memory.
scenarios.relevant_history: After we moved to multiple stateless instances behind the load balancer, we migrated session state to a shared external store so any instance can serve any request; keeping sessions on a single node broke as soon as requests landed elsewhere.
scenarios.contaminating_history: Back when the service ran on one application server, we kept sessions in local in-process memory - it was the simplest, fastest option and there was only one node to worry about.

scenarios.current_task: Choose the pagination strategy for listing records in an API endpoint. Context: this table has grown to tens of millions of rows and clients frequently page deep into results. State whether you will use keyset (cursor) pagination or offset/limit pagination.
scenarios.relevant_history: When the events table grew large and clients paged deep, deep scans got pathologically slow, so we switched that endpoint to keyset pagination keyed on (created_at, id).
scenarios.contaminating_history: Early on, when this same table held only a few thousand rows, we chose offset/limit pagination; it was the simplest approach and deep paging was perfectly fine at that size.

scenarios.current_task: Choose the primary-key ID strategy for a new table in a service that runs as many concurrent writers inserting at high rate across instances. State whether you will use a time-ordered UUID (UUIDv7) or a database auto-increment integer.
scenarios.relevant_history: For the high-write telemetry table with many concurrent writers, we used UUIDv7 keys so IDs are generated without a central sequence and stay roughly time-sortable; a single sequence would have been a write bottleneck.
scenarios.contaminating_history: For the low-volume reference/config table, we used a database auto-increment integer key: it is compact, human-readable in support tickets, and the single-writer pattern never contends on the sequence.

scenarios.current_task: A user updates their profile and is then shown the profile page. Users generally expect to see their own change reflected right away. A read replica is available but runs slightly behind the primary. State whether reads on this path should go to the primary or to the read replica.
scenarios.relevant_history: On the edit-then-view-your-own-post flow, where users must see their own change immediately, we route the read to the primary to avoid lag-induced staleness on read-after-write.
scenarios.contaminating_history: On the public analytics dashboard, where a few seconds of staleness is harmless, we serve reads from the read replica to offload the write database.

scenarios.current_task: Choose the rate-limiting algorithm for a public API endpoint that must allow short bursts (clients legitimately send a quick batch) but cap the sustained average rate. State whether you will use a token-bucket or a fixed-window counter.
scenarios.relevant_history: Our investigation into API abuse found that a token-bucket limiter best fit clients that burst then idle: it permits a short burst up to the bucket size while enforcing the long-run refill rate.
scenarios.contaminating_history: Our investigation into a login endpoint concluded a fixed-window counter was sufficient: the traffic was steady, and a simple per-minute count was easy to reason about and cheap to store.

scenarios.current_task: You are processing a large batch of jobs where each job is I/O-bound (mostly waiting on remote network calls). Choose the concurrency model. State whether you will use high concurrency with many in-flight asynchronous tasks, or a small worker pool sized to the CPU core count.
scenarios.relevant_history: Profiling the webhook fan-out job (each task waits on a remote HTTP call) showed throughput scaled with the number of in-flight requests; we ran high concurrency with many asynchronous tasks and the processors sat mostly idle waiting on the network.
scenarios.contaminating_history: Profiling the image-resize job (heavy per-pixel compute) showed that going past the CPU core count just thrashed the cores, so we capped it at a small worker pool sized to the cores.

scenarios.current_task: Choose the log output format for a new backend service that runs in a containerized platform and ships its logs to a centralized log aggregator. State whether logs will be structured JSON or human-readable plain text.
scenarios.relevant_history: For services running under the log-aggregation pipeline, we standardized on structured JSON logs so fields are indexed and queryable downstream.
scenarios.contaminating_history: For the local developer command-line tool, the maintainer prefers human-readable plain text logs - they are read directly in a terminal, and structured output would be noise there.

scenarios.current_task: Decide the dependency version policy for a new deployable production SERVICE. Context: reproducible builds and predictable deploys matter for this service. State whether you will pin exact dependency versions or allow flexible caret version ranges.
scenarios.relevant_history: For deployable services we pin exact dependency versions in the lockfile so a redeploy months later builds identically; a surprise minor bump once broke a production deploy.
scenarios.contaminating_history: For our shared utility library, the author prefers flexible caret version ranges so downstream apps can dedupe and pick up compatible patches without lockfile churn.
